answer_text.text: Enzymes lower the activation energy required for a given chemical reaction to occur.
Without an enzyme acting as a catalyst, a much larger investment of energy is needed to ignite a chemical reaction, whereas with the help of an enzyme, less energy is needed for a reaction to begin.
Enzymes only reduce the activation energy required to reach the transition state; they lower the reaction's activation energy but do not change the reaction's free energy.
The enzyme-substrate complex can lower the activation energy by contorting substrate molecules in such a way as to facilitate bond-breaking, helping to reach the transition state.
The enzyme-substrate complex can also lower activation energy by compromising the bond structure so that it is easier to break.
Enzymes can also lower activation energies by taking part in the chemical reaction itself, and in these cases the enzyme will always return to its original state at the reaction's completion.

Because the rates of biochemical reactions are controlled by activation energy, and enzymes lower and determine activation energies for chemical reactions, the relative amounts and functioning of the variety of enzymes within a cell ultimately determine which reactions will proceed and at which rates.
